claims.text: The initial system is a zirconium-alloy fuel-cladding substrate with an elemental Cr coating deposited by PVD.
A CrN interlayer thinner than approximately 0.5 μm is to be reactively sputtered onto the polished zirconium-alloy surface before deposition of elemental Cr.
A thin CrN interlayer will inhibit Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Inhibiting Cr–Zr interdiffusion with the CrN interlayer will prevent premature coating failure.
The CrN-interlayered coating will retain oxidation protection in subcritical water near 280°C for approximately 1000 hours.
The CrN-interlayered coating will retain oxidation protection in steam near 1100°C for approximately 60 seconds.
The CrN layer acts as a diffusion sink or obstacle to Cr and Zr atoms at the coating–substrate interface.
CrN is chemically stable under the proposed exposure conditions.
CrN is thermally stable under the proposed exposure conditions, including the 1100°C steam transient.
The CrN interlayer reduces the interfacial diffusivity of Cr atoms.
The CrN interlayer reduces the interfacial diffusivity of Zr atoms.
Reduced Cr–Zr interdiffusion preserves the integrity of the elemental Cr coating.
Preserving Cr-coating integrity maintains oxidation protection during both exposure regimes.
Relative to Cr deposited directly on zirconium alloy, the CrN-interlayered coating will exhibit significantly less Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the CrN-interlayered coating will retain its integrity for longer.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the CrN-interlayered coating will have improved oxidation resistance in both long-duration subcritical water and transient high-temperature steam.
Exposure in water near 280°C for approximately 1000 hours represents the proposed normal subcritical-water boundary.
Exposure in steam near 1100°C for approximately 60 seconds represents the proposed accident-relevant boundary.
